title: Cost-of-living riots in Milan, Turin and Bologna
deck: Two days of looting around Milan's Duomo grew into protests in about ten Italian cities, landing on a government that has little room to ease prices and an election due in 2027.

fuel.title: Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe
fuel.how: Same-weekend marches in France and riots in Milan show a shared squeeze on prices, rents and wages, and each wave of footage feeds the next.

fuel.title: Online network accused of mobilising Milan rioters
fuel.how: Italian police detained a Moroccan journalist suspected of running the social media movement against rising living costs, which turns an economic grievance into a law-and-order story.

fuel.title: Clashes spread to about ten Italian cities
fuel.how: Water cannons in Rome, clashes in Turin and Bologna, and soldiers guarding central Milan widened the unrest beyond one square.

fuel.title: Iran war keeps pump prices high
fuel.how: Oil and freight costs have stayed elevated since strikes on Iran began on 28 February 2026, and fuel is the most visible price in the protesters' complaints.

fuel.title: Italian spreads widened with France's
fuel.how: Higher borrowing costs in early October, moving in step with French stress, leave Rome less money to ease the price anger behind the riots.

card.headline: Italy's riots are a price-anger story that the government is answering with order, not money

keyNumber.label: arrested over the first two days of rioting in Milan, 17-18 October; later headlines put detentions at 371, 110 of them teens

forYou.line: Expect closures and heavy police and army presence in central Milan, Rome, Turin and Bologna on protest days; shops near the Duomo were looted.
Italian bond spreads moved with France's in early October; watch them against Germany for a political-risk signal.
Brief staff on protest days and check insurance cover for riot damage.
The deeper issue is prices. Fuel, rents and wages are the stated grievances, and the Iran war keeps the first of those high.

effects.text: Two days of looting and clashes around Milan's Duomo; more than 200 arrests; clashes in Turin and Bologna
Protests spread to about ten cities; water cannons used in Rome; soldiers guard central Milan
Police detain a Moroccan journalist suspected of being behind the online network that mobilised protesters
Protesters cite rising prices, fuel most visibly; the Iran war keeps oil and pump prices elevated
Italian bond spreads widened in step with France's in early October
Meloni calls a security meeting and frames the response around order; early headlines call her security operation a first-test success
Less fiscal room to ease household costs while borrowing costs are higher
Retail, tourism and insurance take direct losses and higher security spending in city centres
Debate over online organisation and foreign involvement shifts attention from wages and prices to policing
Disorder before the 2027 parliamentary vote tends to favour whoever promises order, and Meloni is positioning on it
Shared grievances across France, Italy, Belgium and Albania raise the odds of copycat unrest across Europe
If France's debt stress deepens, Italian spreads could widen again and squeeze Rome's budget further
Italy and France vote in 2027 and take opposite lines on Ukraine, so unrest now shapes how united Europe's right stays on Russia

whatHappened: On 17 and 18 October 2026, rioting and looting hit the area around Milan's Duomo. More than 200 people were arrested over the two days, according to the event summary. A Euronews headline reports more than 200 arrests on the second day alone. Clashes followed in Turin and Bologna.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called a security meeting. By 25 October, protests had spread to about ten Italian cities. Water cannons were used in Rome, riot police clashed with demonstrators in Turin and Bologna, and soldiers guarded central Milan. One headline reports demonstrators storming the Colosseum in Rome. We could not confirm the details.

On 25 and 26 October, headlines reported that Italian authorities had detained a Moroccan journalist suspected of being behind the social media network that mobilised the protests. Two outlets also headline allegations of a Hamas funding link, which we could not verify. A Gulf News headline puts the total at 371 detained, 110 of them teenagers. The scope of that count is unclear.
whyItMatters: Living costs. The protesters' grievances are prices, rents and wages. They erupted the same weekend as French marches of about 550,000 people, and each helps explain the other, though neither caused it. Protests spread across Europe, with clashes in Paris and looting in Milan. If the squeeze eases, both countries calm. If it does not, copycat unrest is likely.

Energy. Strikes on Iran that began on 28 February 2026 have kept oil and freight costs high for eight months. Fuel is the price Italians see every time they fill up, and it is the one demonstrators cite most. Rome has little control over it.

Markets. Italian bond spreads widened with France's in early October. France pays about 140 basis points over Germany, and Moody's reviewed its rating on 23 October. We have no outcome in our material. Higher interest costs leave Rome less to spend on relief, which is what the protesters want.

Politics. Meloni answered with a security meeting and soldiers in the streets. Disorder before a vote tends to favour whoever promises order, so this helps her. Italy votes in 2027. An online organising network is now a police and political story, and that moves attention from wages to policing.
Security. The unrest spread from one square in Milan to about ten cities in a week. It is not yet at the scale of France, but the pattern of weekend clashes with police could repeat.

winners.why: It is positioned on order, and early headlines describe its security operation as passing its first test. Voters' fear of disorder tends to help the party promising order.
Demand for protection and riot cover rises after looting in a high-value retail district.

winners.who: German Bunds and other safe-haven assets
winners.why: Investors favour them when French and Italian risk rises, though the size of the move here is unclear.

losers.why: Looting hit shops around the Duomo and heavy policing disrupts trade; one headline even mocks a looter fleeing with a gelato tray.
The grievances behind the protests are unaddressed: fuel, rents and wages.
Soldiers in central Milan and clashes in Rome, with the Colosseum named in one headline, hurt the image of major destinations.
A debate about order and online organisation crowds out the cost-of-living argument they would prefer to make.

whatsNext: Late October and November: further weekend protests in Italian cities are likely. Watch whether the army stays in city centres.
Proceedings against the detained journalist: a court decision on custody and the charges will shape the story about who organised what.
Italy's 2027 budget and any fuel or household relief measure, set against higher borrowing costs.
Italy's parliamentary election in 2027. The vote will be a test of how far order can beat price anger.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what is the most likely path for Italy's unrest over the next two months?
options: Rolling escalation like France's social winter
Contained simmer: flare-ups on weekends, fading by December
Government relief measures calm the streets
A bond-market shock forces budget cuts
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 45%, is a contained simmer. Grievances persist, the government leans on policing, and flare-ups fade without a national movement. Escalation is the second most likely path, at about 25%.

recap.question: Which city's Duomo was the centre of the first two days of rioting?
Which grievance do protesters cite most visibly, and which global event keeps it high?
options: Rents, because of French bond stress
Fuel prices, because of the Iran war
Wages, because of a Moody's review

recap.question: Why might the riots help Meloni politically?
options: Disorder before a vote tends to favour whoever promises order
She has promised to cut fuel taxes

timeline.title: Strikes on Iran begin
timeline.detail: Oil and freight costs stay elevated for eight months and feed pump-price anger across Europe.

timeline.title: French diesel hits a record EUR 2.41 a litre
timeline.detail: A sign of how far the energy shock has pushed visible prices. Italian pump prices are not in our material.

timeline.title: French bond spread widest since the euro crisis
timeline.detail: In early October Italian spreads widened in step, raising Rome's borrowing costs.

timeline.title: Looting begins around Milan's Duomo
timeline.detail: The same day about 550,000 marched in France. Rioting continues into the next day.

timeline.title: Second day of rioting in Milan
timeline.detail: More than 200 arrests over the two days; clashes in Turin and Bologna.

timeline.title: Meloni calls a security meeting
timeline.detail: The government frames its response around order. Euronews reports the second day of clashes.

timeline.title: Moody's reviews France's rating
timeline.detail: A scheduled decision that matters for Italian spreads. The outcome is not in our material.

timeline.title: Protests reach about ten Italian cities
timeline.detail: Water cannons used in Rome; clashes with police in Turin and Bologna; soldiers guard central Milan; protests in Paris, Tirana and Brussels the same day.

timeline.title: Alleged organiser of an online network detained
timeline.detail: A Moroccan journalist is suspected of being behind the social media movement. A Gulf News headline reports 371 detained, 110 of them teens.

causes.name: Price level versus pay
causes.detail: Households cite rents, prices and wages as the grievance. This is the stated claim in the shared-driver connection with France.

causes.name: Limited fiscal room
causes.detail: Italy's debt burden is large, and higher spreads in early October reduce room to spend on relief. We have no new debt figures in our material.

causes.name: Political polarisation before a vote
causes.detail: Italy votes in 2027, which raises the stakes of any disorder.

causes.name: Online mobilisation
causes.detail: Police suspect a social media network was used to organise protests against the rising cost of living.

causes.name: Same-weekend contagion
causes.detail: Large French marches and Italian riots happened on the same days. This is a shared driver, not cause and effect.

causes.name: Energy shock
causes.detail: The Iran war has kept oil and pump prices high for eight months.

causes.name: Market stress
causes.detail: Italian spreads widened with France's, limiting Rome's room to ease the squeeze.

causes.name: Heavy policing and arrests
causes.detail: Water cannons, soldiers in city centres and hundreds of arrests, many teenagers per one headline, can harden grievances as well as deter.

causes.name: Cross-border momentum
causes.detail: Protests the same weekend in Paris, Tirana and Brussels made the movement look European, not local.

stakeholders.name: Giorgia Meloni and her government
stakeholders.wants: Restore order and avoid a cost-of-living argument ahead of the 2027 vote
stakeholders.leverage: Police, army deployment, control of the budget
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep a visible security presence, stress the online-organiser story, offer targeted relief if costs allow

stakeholders.name: Interior ministry and police
stakeholders.wants: Prevent a repeat of looting in central Milan
stakeholders.leverage: Water cannons, arrests, soldiers in city centres
stakeholders.likelyMove: Heavier presence on protest weekends and more investigation of online networks

stakeholders.name: Protesters and their online network
stakeholders.wants: Lower prices, fuel and rents; wage rises
stakeholders.leverage: Social media reach and weekend turnout in several cities
stakeholders.likelyMove: Continue weekend actions; disruption from arrests may slow organisation or radicalise parts of it

stakeholders.name: Opposition parties
stakeholders.wants: Make prices, not order, the issue ahead of 2027
stakeholders.likelyMove: Condemn violence while pressing the government on household costs

stakeholders.name: Bond investors and the ECB
stakeholders.role: Price and backstop for Italian debt
stakeholders.wants: Fiscal credibility and no contagion from France
stakeholders.likelyMove: Watch France first; the ECB has said intervention is not warranted for France

stakeholders.name: Milan shopkeepers and city authorities
stakeholders.wants: Protection of the commercial centre and compensation
stakeholders.likelyMove: Press for visible policing and damage relief

sectors.sector: Retail and hospitality in Milan and other centres
sectors.why: Looting near the Duomo and heavy policing on protest days cut footfall and raise costs.
Soldiers in central Milan and clashes in Rome damage the image of key destinations, and one headline names the Colosseum.
Demand for guards and riot cover rises; premiums may follow.
Spreads widened with France's in early October; further moves depend on France's rating and the 2027 budget.
The Iran war keeps pump prices high, squeezing margins and drivers, and fuel is the grievance most cited.
Demand for monitoring of online mobilisation and for foreign-interference analysis rises, though evidence of foreign funding is unverified.

dailyLife.effect: Oil and freight costs have stayed elevated for eight months; protesters cite fuel as the most visible rising price.
The same household-budget squeeze that drove French marches is a stated grievance in Italy.
Soldiers guard central Milan and protests hit about ten cities, so expect closures and diversions on protest days.
Tourists in Rome, Milan, Turin and Bologna should check local news; clashes were reported in each.
Higher Italian spreads in early October feed into government and bank borrowing costs; the pass-through to households is not quantified in our material.

scenarios.name: Contained simmer
scenarios.looksLike: Weekend flare-ups in several cities, army presence kept, the online network disrupted by arrests, and protests fade by December.
signposts: Turnout falls from the 25 October levels
Arrests continue but violence stays localised
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Italy stays a stable but distracted partner; the 2027 election is fought on order and prices.

scenarios.name: Rolling spread
scenarios.looksLike: Protests grow, copycat groups emerge, more cities see clashes and French unrest keeps momentum.
signposts: Linkage with French strikes or with Belgian and Albanian protests
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Europe faces a shared cost-of-living wave; gains for populist parties ahead of 2027 votes.

scenarios.name: Relief and calm
scenarios.looksLike: Government announces targeted fuel or household relief and talks with organisers; the movement splinters.
signposts: Opposition and government agree on a response
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Calmer streets but less fiscal room; markets may charge a modest premium.

scenarios.name: Market and political shock
scenarios.looksLike: A French downgrade or budget failure widens spreads sharply, forcing Rome into cuts that fuel more protests.
signposts: Italian and French spreads spike together
scenarios.effectOnWorld: A eurozone stress test and a harder fight over support.

predictions.text: Street clashes with police will occur in at least one Italian city again in November 2026. Probability 75%.
Italy's government will announce a targeted cost-of-living or fuel relief measure. Probability 45%.
Soldiers will still be deployed in at least one major Italian city centre in mid-November. Probability 55%.
No Italian protest will reach the size of France's 17 October marches of about 550,000. Probability 85%.
Prosecutors will not publicly substantiate the Hamas-funding allegations with charges against the detained journalist. Probability 70%.

actions: Brief staff and customers on protest days in Milan, Rome, Turin and Bologna.
Check riot and civil-commotion cover and the documentation needed for claims.
Add buffer time for deliveries into city centres on likely protest weekends.
Review contracts for fuel-surcharge and force-majeure clauses.
Track the Italian-German spread alongside the French one; they moved together in early October.
Treat Italian political risk as tied to France's rating and budget news until it passes.
Do not assume an ECB backstop; for France the ECB has said intervention is not warranted.
Plan travel around protest days and follow local advice.
Expect fuel and living costs to stay high while the Iran war continues.
Where possible, fix borrowing costs before any further spread widening.
Separate policing of violence from the underlying price grievances.
Publish who benefits from any relief measure to counter an austerity or order-only narrative.
Coordinate with France, Belgium and other states on shared cost-of-living drivers.

analogues.whatFollowed: A fuel-tax rise was scrapped and concessions followed; the movement faded but grievances did not.
Energy costs weighed on household budgets; the government fell in July and a right-led coalition won the September vote.

analogues.event: Italian sovereign debt stress and the change of government
analogues.whatFollowed: High spreads forced a change of prime minister and austerity; a reminder of how markets can limit Rome's choices.

watch.title: Moody's review of France (outcome not in our material)
watch.why: A downgrade or negative outlook could widen Italian spreads and shrink Rome's room to ease costs.

watch.title: Next protest weekend
watch.why: Turnout and violence will show whether the movement is growing or fading.

watch.title: Court hearings for the detained journalist
watch.why: Custody decisions and the charges will test the online-organiser and foreign-funding claims.

watch.title: Italian and French spreads versus Germany
watch.why: Joint widening signals market contagion and less room for relief.

watch.title: Pump prices and Gulf headlines
watch.why: Renewed oil spikes would reignite the grievance fastest.

watch.title: Italy's 2027 budget law
watch.why: Whether it includes household relief or fuel measures will signal whether Meloni answers with money as well as order.

watch.title: Neighbours
watch.why: Further clashes in Paris, Brussels or Tirana, or new protests elsewhere in Europe, would show the unrest is cross-border.

confidence.note: Event summary says over the two days; the Euronews headline says on the second day. Counting may differ.
From a single headline (Gulf News, 26 October). The scope of the count and the period it covers are not clear.

confidence.claim: Protests in about ten cities, water cannons in Rome, clashes in Turin and Bologna, soldiers in Milan
confidence.note: Consistent across several headlines from 25 October; we did not read full articles.

confidence.claim: A Moroccan journalist was detained as alleged organiser of an online network
confidence.note: Reported by Yabiladi and Brussels Signal as suspicion, not proven. Other outlets call him an academic.

confidence.claim: Hamas funding allegations against the alleged organiser
confidence.note: Appears in partisan outlets' headlines only. We could not verify and do not rely on it.

confidence.claim: Italian spreads widened with France's in early October
confidence.note: Taken from the connected event on French bond stress; the size of the move is not stated in our material.

evidence.method: Drafted from the sources and wire headlines listed, mostly headlines and one article summary, plus the connected events in the knowledge base. We did not read the full text of most articles. Arrest counts, the number of cities and the journalist's detention rest on headlines and are hedged. Allegations of foreign funding are unverified and not used as fact. Scenario probabilities, predictions and the effects of spreads on Italian household relief are the author's estimates.
